<reason>B owned the decision rule the motion actually sets — the default — and steadily narrowed the fight to the entry fee, where its strongest mechanism line ("a price works only by being unaffordable to someone") and its equity-engineering answers (walk-up quotas, lotteries, demand-priced non-gate revenue) survived A's pressure. A's inversion — unpriced overload excludes the nurse by time, queue, and ruin — was genuinely damaging, and A directly answered the ceiling question with a necessity standard, but its claim that concessions/permits/parking can't scale stayed asserted, it misdescribed lotteries as dawn-booking, and it never engaged irreversibility or gave an enforcement answer to the revenue-dependence ratchet. B's "your closing is my opening" was overreach (A did defend gate growth, which is not the motion) and its stray [C1.2]/[C4.x] reference IDs cost grounding credit, but despite A holding the last word in every round, B's path to the ballot was cleaner and the debate easier to decide its way.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The nurse exchange: A's Rebuttal 1 ("rules ration by time and luck… it selects against her") was the debate's best single inversion, but B's Rebuttal 2 answered it with the decisive contrast — caps can hold walk-up quotas and lotteries that cost her nothing, while a price excludes by design — and A never squarely engaged lotteries. Runner-up: B's Rebuttal 1 "you defended tools I already conceded," which forced the entire debate onto the entry fee, the one mechanism A had to win and couldn't.</best_rebuttal>
